audit: The anonymous method accepts an endpoint parameter that flows directly into Storage::Service.new(host), which is assigned to @service.root_url without any validation. This root_url is then used by the Google::Apis storage client to perform HTTP requests to the specified host. As a result, an attacker‑supplied endpoint can be used to redirect API calls to arbitrary hosts, enabling Server‑Side Request Forgery (SSRF). No other parameters influence execution paths that could lead to file system access or remote code execution.

retrieve! passes the user‐supplied identifier directly into uploader.store_path and then File.expand_path, so a crafted identifier containing “../” can escape the uploader.root and read arbitrary files via SanitizedFile.new.

The import method wraps `keydata` in a GPGME::Data via Data.new(keydata), which will open or read from arbitrary IO or filesystem handles (e.g. File or Pathname) if supplied. This lets an attacker force the library to read arbitrary files off disk. The imported data is then fed into gpgme_op_import, but the root cause is unguarded Data.new accepting attacker‑controlled file handles.

params.options: -> fed into Ctx.new(options) for context flags (no direct RCE/SSRF)

audit: The #initialize method takes a user-specified :cluster option and uses URI parsing to extract host, port, scheme, and credentials. Those values are passed to Redis::Client#connect without validating the hostname or port, allowing SSRF to arbitrary TCP services if the input originates from an untrusted source.

The #process method forwards any commands array directly through Node#process to Redis::Client#process without applying the cluster-level send_command filters in #call. This allows injection of administrative or scripting commands (e.g. SHUTDOWN, BGSAVE, CONFIG REWRITE, EVAL), enabling server-side file writes, termination, or script execution.

plantuml_content selects the output format and then, when format='txt' and txt is enabled, delegates to plantuml_txt_content which calls URI.open on a generated URL, resulting in SSRF. The URL is built from user-controlled server_url and diagram code with only HTTP/HTTPS scheme validated, allowing requests to arbitrary endpoints.

This method constructs a URL by concatenating the document’s server_url and user-controlled type, format, encoded text, and opts into the path and query string without validating the host or path segments. A malicious author can set the kroki-server-url or diagram options to induce SSRF to arbitrary endpoints.

The initialize method iterates dynamically over Octokit::Configurable.keys and uses instance_variable_set to assign every option key at runtime, allowing unvalidated input parameters to propagate through the client. Parameters like api_endpoint, connection_options, proxy, and middleware flow into Faraday/Sawyer setup (in Connection.agent and sawyer_options), enabling arbitrary outbound HTTP requests (SSRF). The netrc_file and netrc flags flow into login_from_netrc (Authentication), calling Netrc.read on a user‐supplied path, leading to arbitrary file reads. No sanitization or validation is performed on these critical parameters.
The `get` method accepts a user-supplied `path` which is directly parsed into a URI and used by Net::HTTP without validation, allowing SSRF via attacker-controlled URLs.

request takes a user‑controlled URL parameter and passes it unfiltered to Faraday.build_url and then run_request, executing an HTTP request without host whitelisting or sanitization. This allows an attacker to force server‑side requests to arbitrary endpoints (SSRF).

Factory.create passes user-controlled options (URI strings or Hashes) through extract_addresses_and_options and resolve to extract_host_options_from_uri/extract_host_options_from_hash, which are then fed directly into Redis::Store.new or Redis::DistributedStore.new. This allows attackers to specify arbitrary hostnames, ports, Unix socket paths, and query parameters, enabling SSRF or unauthorized socket access. No sanitization or host whitelisting is applied.

extract_host_options_from_uri parses attacker-controlled URI via URI.parse and CGI.unescape, building host, port, path, db, namespace, username, password, and arbitrary query-based options without validation. The returned hash flows back to the factory and ultimately into the Redis client connection, enabling SSRF to remote hosts or unauthorized local socket file access.

The `directory` accessor triggers `load_directory`, which calls `fetch_directory` and issues an HTTP GET to `@directory_url`. Because `@directory_url` originates from the (user‑controlled) `directory` parameter passed to `initialize`, this path likewise enables SSRF. No sanitization or host‐restriction is applied before fetching the directory data.

The initialize method accepts a user‑supplied `directory` parameter which is converted into a URI and stored in `@directory_url`. That variable is subsequently used by `fetch_directory` to perform an HTTP GET to whatever host the user provided. Since there is no validation or restriction on the directory URL, this allows arbitrary SSRF (Server‑Side Request Forgery).

make_creds hands off unvalidated JSON fields into three credential types that perform unrestricted HTTP(S) calls, arbitrary filesystem reads, and command execution. IdentityPoolCredentials can SSRF via credential_source.url or read any file via credential_source.file. PluggableAuthCredentials can execute any command from credential_source.executable.command and read arbitrary output_file. AwsCredentials pulls AWS metadata from JSON‐controlled URLs (SSRF). Finally, token_url and service_account_impersonation_url permit SSRF in the STS exchange and impersonation endpoints.

A user‑supplied config hash is merged and passed through dynamic eval, allowing arbitrary method invocation via config keys (RCE). The parse_environment_variables method evals options from ENV['RES_OPTIONS'] without sanitization, leading to remote code execution. The parse_config_file uses IO.foreach on config_file to read arbitrary local files. Additionally, passing a custom log_file causes Logger to write to attacker‑controlled file paths.

The start method instantiates a new Resolver and calls search with a user‑controlled name, causing DNS queries via UDP/TCP (SSRF). It also invokes initialize, which includes dynamic eval of ENV['RES_OPTIONS'], enabling RCE at startup. Combined, start can trigger both SSRF and RCE depending on runtime inputs.

MiniMagick::Image.open takes a user‑controlled path_or_url and, via open‑uri, can fetch arbitrary URL schemes (HTTP, FTP, file://), enabling SSRF and local file reads. The fetched data is then written to a Tempfile via IO.copy_stream, resulting in arbitrary file writes under the process’s tmpdir. The ext parameter flows unchecked into Utilities.tempfile to control the temporary file extension, and the options hash is forwarded verbatim into open-uri or Pathname.open. No sanitization is performed, so untrusted URLs or file paths can be abused to read remote or local resources.

params.options: passed directly to open-uri or Pathname.open
params.ext: passed to Utilities.tempfile to set the temp‐file extension

audit: The class method open accepts caller‑supplied host, port, and hosts parameters and passes them directly into new_connection and Connection#open_connection, allowing TCP connections to arbitrary endpoints (SSRF). It also accepts an :encryption hash with tls_options (e.g. :ca_file) that is fed into OpenSSL::SSLContext#set_params, enabling arbitrary file reads. There is no validation or restriction on hostnames, ports, or file paths.

Asciidoctor.convert accepts user‑controlled input and options that can lead to arbitrary file writes if safe mode is lowered, as well as SSRF via the allow‑uri‑read attribute. The :to_file, :to_dir, :mkdirs, and :base_dir options drive normalize_system_path and Helpers.mkdir_p to write output anywhere when options[:safe] < SafeMode::SAFE. User attributes ['allow‑uri‑read'] enable OpenURI.open_uri calls (SSRF) and ['data‑uri'] allows embedding remote or local content. The convert pipeline’s stylesheet copy ([‘copycss’,‘linkcss’]) can read and write arbitrary files when enabled. Data flow spans lib/asciidoctor/convert.rb, load.rb, abstract_node.rb, path_resolver.rb, document.rb and the HTML5 converter.

Asciidoctor.convert_file simply opens the given filename for reading and delegates to Asciidoctor.convert, thus allowing arbitrary local file reads via the filename parameter. All convert vulnerabilities (file write, SSRF, stylesheet copy, data‑uri embedding) apply downstream. The initial File.open and input.read in load.rb expose local file disclosure, and no further sandboxing is applied.

The resolve call delegates to multiple credential providers based on config (and ENV). Several paths expose dangerous operations: static_profile_process_credentials / process_credentials can invoke an external process (credential_process) via ProcessCredentials, leading to arbitrary command execution; instance_profile_credentials uses ECSCredentials with AWS_CONTAINER_CREDENTIALS_FULL_URI, and although HTTP scheme URIs are locked to loopback, HTTPS URIs are not validated, allowing SSRF to arbitrary hosts; assume_role_web_identity_credentials and shared‐config based assume_role_web_identity_credentials_from_config accept AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE or config file paths and read them directly, allowing arbitrary local file reads; likewise ECSCredentials may read AWS_CONTAINER_AUTHORIZATION_TOKEN_FILE. All these flows originate from resolve’s config or environment inputs.
info(progname, &block) behaves like add(), writing progname or block output to the log file unchecked.

The 'message' parameter (or 'progname' when message is omitted) flows directly into LogDevice.write without sanitization via format_message, leading to arbitrary file writes. The block-yielded message is also written unchecked. No network or command execution is involved.
log is an alias for add(), so any inputs behave identically to add(): writes untrusted message or progname to disk without sanitization.

debug(progname, &block) forwards progname or block output to add(), which writes it to the log file without sanitization. Untrusted strings passed as progname or via the block will be written to disk.

The 'logdev' parameter flows into LogDevice.new -> open_logfile -> File.open/create_logfile, enabling arbitrary file creation/appending. The 'shift_period_suffix' parameter is used directly in log rotation to build file rename targets, which can lead to path traversal if untrusted strings are provided.

The formatter setter takes the provided 'formatter' object (often a proc) and stores it; this proc is later called on each log entry via format_message, allowing arbitrary code execution if attacker-controlled.

params.formatter: @formatter.call(severity, time, progname, msg) -> arbitrary code execution

audit: warn(progname, &block) forwards inputs to add(), writing them to the log file without sanitization.
error(progname, &block) forwards inputs to add(), causing arbitrary file writes of progname or block output to the log file.
